sentences.text: Tecovasuchus is an extinct genus belonging to the aetosaur family.
This animal is distinguished by osteoderms—bony plates embedded in the skin—with thickened, beveled edges, deep pits, radiating grooves, and tongue-shaped dorsal flanges.
Before its formal description, fossils attributed to Tecovasuchus were previously classified as Paratypothorax or similar aetosaurs.
Tecovasuchus serves as an index taxon for the St. Johnsian sub-LVF, helping correlate Late Triassic localities in the southwestern United States.
Tecovasuchus belongs to the parent group Paratypothoracisini.
It is classified within the family Stagonolepididae.
Tecovasuchus lived during the Norian stage, between 227.3 and 205.7 million years ago.
Fossils are primarily found in the Late Triassic Tecovas Formation in Texas, dating to the lower Norian stage.
Remains have also been discovered in the Chinle Group in New Mexico and Arizona, ranging from Carnian to Rhaetian ages.
Specimens have been collected from the Tecovas Formation, Bluewater Creek Formation, and the Los Esteros Member of the Santa Rosa Formation.
